finding: There is no live range for this job yet, so this is a first build. Built totals, labor only (no parts), stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Hyundai Elantra about $96-$176 (0.8-1.1 hr); midsize 2017 Honda CR-V about $96-$176 (0.8-1.1 hr); truck 2021 Ram 1500 about $132-$176 (1.1 hr); luxury 2017 Genesis G80 about $132-$176 (1.1 hr). Across classes that is roughly $96-$176. How this compares: the built range sits on the consumer guides ($100-$200 and $100-$175 for a four-wheel alignment) and on one dealer menu ($139.95-$169.95), and below RepairPal's national average of $186-$273 (F-150 $188-$276, Silverado $166-$243, Accord $157-$231, Camry $223-$326). So the build is about right for a chain or independent shop and low for a dealer; a shown range of about $100-$250 would cover both. Candidly, an alignment is sold at a menu price, not billed by the hour. Chains often sell it below a book-time build as a coupon item or bundle it with tires, and sell lifetime plans at about the price of two alignments, while dealers and shops that calibrate driver-assist cameras charge above it. Our hours are manufacturer warranty times, the low end of what a shop bills. How solid the labor times are: every class now has a maker-printed time, and six of the eight range ends are for the example vehicle itself. Economy: Hyundai's all-models 1.1 hr (covers the Elantra; includes diagnosis), with Honda's 0.8 hr for a CR-V as the low end; no second economy-car figure was found. Midsize: Honda's 0.8 hr for the 2017-20 CR-V itself, with Hyundai's 1.1 hr as the high end. Truck (second look, 2026-11-20): the example moved from the F-150, for which no time exists, to the 2021 Ram 1500, where FCA prints 1.1 hr for 'Perform Front Wheel Alignment' as a stand-alone operation (unsold vehicles) in two bulletins, for the 2020 and 2021 trucks. That is the same 1.1 hr the class carried before, so the totals do not move, but it is now a truck maker's figure for the example truck. It is a front alignment, which is the whole adjustment on a pickup with a solid rear axle, and the bulletin does not list its steps. FCA's 1.3 hr for the same job with a road test, Toyota's 1.5 hr for a Tundra (with a tread-depth inspection and paperwork), GM's 0.9 hr add-on for a 2025 Silverado, Ford's 0.8 hr to correct front toe on an F-150 and FCA's 1.1 hr to replace a heavy-duty Ram's steering linkage and set toe are all cross-checks: each covers more or less than a stand-alone alignment, and together they put a pickup at roughly 0.8-1.5 hr. A truck quote at the top of that spread would build to about $240, above our range. Luxury: Genesis's 1.1 hr for the 2017-18 G80 itself (includes diagnosis). No second stand-alone luxury time was found: Acura prints 0.4 hr for a four-wheel alignment in two bulletins (TLX, RLX), but both times are billed on top of another repair, and the Infiniti and Acura bulletins that call for a four-wheel alignment either fold it into a larger operation or refer to the flat rate manual. No European luxury time was found; BMW and Mercedes alignments, which often need ride-height weighting or camera calibration, may cost more than this build. The Tesla service-manual figures (0.90 for the Model 3 and Model Y, 1.26 for the Cybertruck) are printed without a unit and stay cross-checks. Still weak: truck and luxury are single-figure ranges; the Hyundai and Genesis time includes diagnosis; and nothing here is a shop's book time. Not found: a chain shop's own posted alignment price and an alignment-equipment maker's stated time. A front-only (two-wheel) alignment on a car is a smaller job, about $50-$100 in the guides. Seized adjusters, cam bolts, shims and worn parts are extra, and an alignment cannot be finished on worn tie rods or ball joints. Reviewer note 2026-11-20: confidence kept low. The Hyundai/Genesis 1.1 hr is titled alignment diagnosis and repair, the Ram 1.1 hr is a front alignment on unsold new trucks, truck and luxury are single figures, and no shop book time or European luxury time was found.
extras: A quote may add: freeing or replacing seized adjusters, eccentric (cam) bolts or sleeves; camber or caster shims or adjustment kits on vehicles with no factory adjustment; worn tie rod ends, ball joints, bushings or wheel bearings that must be replaced before the alignment will hold; a steering angle sensor reset; calibration of driver-assist cameras or radar on newer vehicles (can cost more than the alignment itself); extra labor for lifted, lowered or modified vehicles; an alignment check or inspection fee if no adjustment is made; shop supplies and sales tax. Lifetime or multi-year alignment plans cost more up front. Ask for the before-and-after printout.
